title: Nothing to take
hookLine: no one could enslave Diogenes, because he'd let go of everything they could take
carry: how much of you someone could take

lines: A PICKPOCKET READS WHAT YOU CLUTCH.
AN OLD MAN WITH AN EMPTY BAG.
cards: A pickpocket works a crowded market. He's good. He reads people by what they clutch: the bag held tight, the hand that keeps checking the back pocket.
Then he passes an old man in a torn cloak, with an empty bag and a stick, sitting on the steps, laughing at something. The pickpocket walks right by. There's nothing to work with.
Epictetus holds up this old man, Diogenes, as a picture of a free person, in the middle of that same long talk on freedom.

teach.b: From the day Diogenes learned from his teacher Antisthenes, Epictetus says in book four, chapter one, no one could make him a slave again. Not because of his birth or a document, but because of how he held things.
Here's a way to see it: everything you own has a handle. Your money, your reputation, even your body. Anyone who wants power over you grabs the handle you care most about and pulls.
In Epictetus' telling, Diogenes held his things so loosely there was nothing to grab. Take the cloak, take the bag, even threaten the body: he'd give them up rather than give up himself.
Diogenes Laertius, a later collector of stories about the philosophers, says Diogenes was once captured by pirates and put up for sale. Asked what he could do, he said: govern men.
Sell me, he said, to someone who needs a master. Nobody knows whether it happened. It's the kind of story told about a person because it fits.
The honest catch: this isn't a lesson in owning nothing. A life comes with kids, rent and a job, and Epictetus isn't asking anyone to walk away from them. The point is the grip.
You can live in a house without being held by it. You can love a reputation without being leashed to it. The question is never how much you have.
It's how much of you someone could take by taking it.

how: People who practice Stoicism sometimes rehearse letting go of possessions, roles or reputation in their minds, so that losing them would not mean losing themselves.

o: a thinker who taught that owning things is evil
a Stoic who gave all he owned to the poor
a Cynic who held things too loosely to grab

games.q: nothing to take — tap the pairs.
p: the teacher who freed Diogenes' mind
what others grab to control you
what Epictetus asks us to loosen

s: Epictetus says you must own nothing to be free
the point is how tightly you hold, not how much you own.

with nothing he clutched, there was nothing for anyone to pull.

games.q: you're Diogenes, captured by pirates and standing at the slave market. the auctioneer asks what you can do. what do you say?
o: say you can govern men, and ask to be sold to someone who needs a master.
games.why: in the story told by Diogenes Laertius, he says he can govern men. even on the auction block, there's nothing they can take.

practice: Make a tight fist, as if holding something you're afraid to lose, and silently name it: my phone, my plans, what they think of me. Now slowly open the hand, palm up, on your knee.
The thing is still yours; only the grip has changed, and an open hand can still hold, but can't be pried.

wordCard.voice: Diogenes. Epictetus' picture of a free person: he held everything so loosely that there was no handle left for anyone to grab.

carryVoice: Your line: how much of you someone could take. Less grip, less handle. Until tomorrow.
